[Page 613]

The opening of this surah with the command to say (*qul*) serves to draw attention to what follows the act of saying, as you know from His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1].

This command in this surah has another benefit: it was revealed in response to the words of the polytheists, "Describe your Lord to us (*insub lana rabbaka*)." It was therefore an answer to their question, and for this reason he was told "Say" (*qul*), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: The Spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 85]. So the command to perform the act of saying (*qul*) has two benefits.

The pronoun *huwa* ("He") is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), to convey emphasis on the sentence that follows it. When those who asked heard it, they looked forward to what came after it.

It is also permissible for *huwa* to refer back to the Lord, in the question of the polytheists when they said, "Describe your Lord to us."

Some scholars counted the pronoun *huwa* in this surah as one of the Most Beautiful Names of God (*al-asma' al-husna*). This is a Sufi method, followed by Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in his explanation of the Most Beautiful Names. Ibn 'Arafa transmitted it from him in his tafsir, and al-Fakhr mentioned it in *Mafatih al-Ghayb*. It is necessary to combine the two statements.

The essence of both is his statement: ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾. In it there are three names of God, exalted is He, as an indication of three stations.

The first: the station of the foremost, those brought near, who look at the realities of things in terms of what they are in themselves. Therefore they saw no existent other than God, for He is the One for whose sake existence is necessary; so, for them, whatever is other than God is non-existent. Thus his saying "*Huwa*" is an unrestricted indication. Since the one indicated is specific, that unrestricted reference is directed to that specific one. So "*huwa*" was an indication from these brought-near ones to God, and they did not need a distinguishing qualifier in that indication. The word "*huwa*" was therefore sufficient for these people to attain complete knowledge.

The second station is that of the companions of the right, the moderate ones. They witnessed the Truth as existent and witnessed possible things as existent, so multiplicity arose among existents. Thus the word "*huwa*" was not fully sufficient for them, so they needed a distinguishing qualifier with it. For their sake it was said: ﴿He is God﴾.

The third station is that of the companions of the left, who permit the plurality of gods. So the word "*ahad*" (One) was joined to his saying "He is God," as a refutation of their claim. End of quotation.

As for His name, the proper name (*al-'alam*), it was mentioned first, before the predicates were applied to it, so that this would be a way of recalling all His attributes when Muslims converse and when they dispute with the polytheists. This name is well known among all Arabs; its referent's existence is not disputed, but they used to describe Him with attributes from which He is exempt.

As for "*ahad*," it is a noun meaning "one" (*wahid*). Its original root letter is *waw*, so it is said *wahad*, just as *ahad* is said. The *waw* was changed into a hamza (*ahad*) contrary to analogy, since it is vowelled with a fatha (unlike the change of the *waw* in *wujuh*). Its meaning is "alone, singular." Al-Nabigha said:

"As if my saddle, when the day had passed for us at Dhu al-Jalil, was on a wild bull, startled by a human, and alone, separated from his herd."

That is: as if I had put my foot on a wild bull who sensed a human and was alone, apart from his herd.

It is an attributive adjective (*sifa mushabbaha*) like *hasan* (good). It is said *wahud* like *karum*, and *wahid* like *farih*.

The form of the attributive adjective indicates that the attribute is firmly established in the one described, as an intrinsic property of it. Therefore "*ahad*" was preferred here over "*wahid*," because "*wahid*" is an active participle, which does not indicate firm establishment. So "*wahid*" and "*ahad*" are two attributes derived by inflection from one root, the root of unity, meaning singularity.

This is the basic sense of its usage, and from it branched out usages that became established meanings of the word "*ahad*." The most famous is that it is used as a noun meaning "a person" specifically in negation, as in His saying: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqara: 285], in al-Baqara, and His saying: ﴿And I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 38], in al-Kahf. Likewise, it is used for the numeral in counting, as in *ahada 'ashara* (eleven) and *ahad wa 'ishrin* (twenty-one). Its feminine is *ihda*. Some scholars confused "*wahid*" with "*ahad*," and fell into confusion.

So the description of God as "*ahad*" means that He is singular in the reality that is considered in His proper name, namely the well-known divinity. When it is said ﴿God is One (*ahad*)﴾, the meaning is that He is singular in divinity. When it is said "God is one (*wahid*)," the meaning is that He is one, not multiple, and whoever is other than Him is not a god. The outcome of the two descriptions is the negation of a partner to Him, exalted is He, in His divinity.

Since at the beginning of the mission it was intended to establish complete unity for God, as instruction for all people and as a refutation of the doctrine of polytheism, God was described in this surah as "*ahad*" and was not described as "*wahid*." This is because the attributive adjective is the furthest that can bring the meaning of God's oneness close to the minds of the people of clear Arabic speech.

Ibn Sina said in a commentary of his on this surah: "*Ahad*" indicates that He, exalted is He, is one in every respect, and that there is no multiplicity in Him at all, neither notional multiplicity, which is the multiplicity of constituents, genera and differentiae, nor sensory multiplicity, which is the multiplicity of distinct external parts conceived by the intellect, as in matter and form, and sensory multiplicity, potential or actual, as in a body. That implies that He, glory be to Him, is exempt from genus and differentia, matter and form, accidents and parts, limbs and shapes, colours, and all else that would impair complete unity and true simplicity, which befit the nobility of His Face, mighty and majestic, such that anything resembles Him or equals Him, glory be to Him. Its explanation: As for the "one," it is predicated of what falls under it by gradation (*tashkik*). That which is not divisible in any respect at all is more worthy of oneness than that which is divisible in some respects. That which is not divisible by intellectual division is more worthy of oneness than that which is divisible by sensory division, potentially and then actually. So "*ahad*" comprises the indication of oneness in every respect, and that there is no multiplicity in the one described. End of quotation.

I say: The Muslims understood this. It is narrated that Bilal, when he was tortured for Islam, would say: "*Ahad, ahad*." And the slogan of the Muslims on the day of Badr was: "*Ahad, ahad*."

What most researchers into the names of God have followed is that "*ahad*" is not counted among the Most Beautiful Names, because its mention did not occur in the hadith of Abu Hurayra in al-Tirmidhi. He said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God has ninety-nine names; whoever counts them enters Paradise." He enumerated them and did not mention the attribute "*ahad*" among them, but mentioned the attribute "*wahid*." On this basis Imam al-Haramayn proceeded in *Kitab al-Irshad* and *Kitab al-Luma'*, and al-Ghazali in his explanation of the Most Beautiful Names.

Al-Fihri said in his commentary on Imam al-Haramayn's *Luma' al-Adilla*, when mentioning God's name "*al-Wahid*" (the One): "*Ahad*" occurs in some narrations, but he did not combine the two names into one name.

Ibn Barrajan al-Ishbili in his explanation of the Names, and Shaykh Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Kumi (with a *mim*) al-Tunisi, and Lutf Allah al-Arzarumi in *Ma'arij al-Nur*, followed the counting of *ahad* among the Most Beautiful Names along with its name "*al-Wahid*." They said: "*al-Wahid al-Ahad*," such that it is like an emphasis on it, as their counting of the names as ninety-nine implies. This is based on the view that the hadith of Abu Hurayra does not require confining the Most Beautiful Names to ninety-nine, but is only to explain the virtue of those counted names within it.

The meaning is that God is singular in divinity; nothing among existents shares it with Him. This is a refutation of the polytheism held by the polytheists, of the Trinity invented by the Melkite Christians, of the dualism of the Magians, and of the countless multiplicity of the Brahmins.

So his saying ﴿God is One (*ahad*)﴾ is the counterpart of his saying in another verse ﴿God is only one God (*ilah wahid*)﴾ [al-Nisa': 171]. This is the meaning that the addressees in this verse, who were asking about the lineage of God, that is, His reality, would grasp. So it was begun for them by saying He is one, so that they would know that the idols have no share in divinity at all.

Then, oneness necessarily entails existence, so the view of the deniers (*mu'attila*) and the materialists (*dahriyya*) is refuted.

The scholars of kalam (scholastic theology) from among the People of the Sunna agreed on deriving the negative divine attributes from the meaning of oneness. For if He is singular in divinity, He is independent of anything that specifies Him by bringing into existence. For if He needed one who brought Him into being, then the one who brought Him into being would be a god prior to Him. Therefore God's existence is eternal, not preceded by nonexistence, and does not need one who specifies His existence in place of nonexistence. He is self-sufficient for continuance through existence, so He is everlasting. He is independent of other than Himself. He is unlike created things, for otherwise He would need a specifier just as they do. Thus describing Him, exalted is He, as "*ahad*" comprises the negative attributes. The same is said of its synonym, which is a single attribute (*wasf wahid*).

They agreed that God's oneness is a necessary and complete oneness: God, exalted is He, is one in every respect, and under every assumption there is no multiplicity at all in the essence of God. Neither is there notional multiplicity, which is the plurality of constituents, of genera and differentiae from which quiddities are composed, nor is there multiplicity of external parts from which bodies are composed. Thus the description "*ahad*" conveys that He is exempt from genus and differentia, matter and form, accidents and parts, limbs, shapes and colours, and all that is contrary to complete oneness, as Ibn Sina indicated.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: "In the reading of the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿God is One﴾ without *qul huwa*." End of quotation. He probably took it from what is narrated: the Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever recites (*Allahu ahad*) it is equal to a third of the Qur'an." He mentioned it along with the report of the reading of Ubayy without "*qul*," which al-Tibi interpreted, saying: "This is evidence for this reading."

In my view, if the reading narrated is authentic, then the Prophet ﷺ did not intend it as recitation, but intended to comply with what he was commanded to say. This is like how he used to frequently say: "Glory be to my Lord the Great and with His praise, O God, forgive me," interpreting His saying: ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness﴾ [al-Nasr: 3].

[Page 617]

﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ is a second sentence, quoted by the same speech as the sentence ﴿Allah is One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]. So it is a second predicate about the pronoun. A predicate may be repeated, and it may be joined by a conjunction or left unjoined. Here it is separated from the preceding sentence because these sentences are offered as instruction for the listeners. Each sentence was therefore fit to stand on its own, not attached to the one before it by a conjunction. This follows the method of presenting issues to a student, as when one says: "Possession (al-hawz) is a condition for the validity of detention (al-habs). Possession is not complete except by direct observation." Or as when one says: "Antarah is among the stallions of poets. Antarah is among the champions of knights."

For this reason the Name of Majesty (Allah) is stated explicitly in ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾. The expected form by ordinary usage would have been: "He is the Eternal Refuge."

Al-samad: the lord (sayyid) on whom one cannot dispense in important matters, and the chief of a people whom they obey.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: it is the form fa'al in the sense of maf'ul, from "samada ilayhi," meaning he went to him intending him. So al-samad is the one who is sought in needs.

I say: its counterpart is al-sanad (the support), to which important matters are referred. Also al-falaq is a name for the morning, because the night is split (yatafallaq) away from it.

Al-samad is one of the attributes of Allah. Allah is the true Eternal Refuge, complete in the quality of being sought, in an absolute and general sense.

Al-samad is among the ninety-nine Names in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah narrated by al-Tirmidhi. Its meaning is: the one on whom everything other than Him depends. The non-existent depends on Him for its existence, and the existent depends on Him in its affairs.

The expressions of the early exegetes (al-salaf) about the meaning of al-samad are numerous, and all of them fall under this comprehensive meaning. Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi) reduced them to eighteen opinions. This Name also includes Allah's relational attributes of meaning: that He is Living, Knowing, Willing, Powerful, Speaking, Hearing, and Seeing. For if any one of these attributes were absent from Him, He would not be one to whom one turns for need.

[Page 618]

The form of ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ is a form of restriction (qasr), by means of defining the predicate. It therefore establishes that the quality of being the Eternal Refuge is restricted to Allah, the Exalted. This is a restriction by reversal (qasr qalb), intended to nullify what the people of polytheism were accustomed to in the Age of Ignorance: calling upon their idols for their needs, and turning to them in their calamities, until they forgot Allah.

Abu Sufyan said, on the night of the Conquest of Mecca, while he was in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Has the time not yet come for you to testify that there is no god but Allah? I know that if there were another god with Him, it would have profited me nothing."

﴿لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ﴾

The clause ﴿لَمْ يَلِدْ﴾ ("He begets not") is a second predicate of the divine name ﴿اللَّهُ﴾ ("Allah") in His saying ﴿اللَّهُ الصَّمَدُ﴾ ("Allah, the Eternal Refuge") [al-Ikhlas: 2]. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject) of the subject, or a comprehensive substitution (badal ishtimal) for the clause ﴿اللَّهُ الصَّمَدُ﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2]. This is because one to whom recourse is made (al-samad) cannot be in a state where he begets, since the desire for a child is for the purpose of seeking help from the child in managing the affairs of the parent and making up for the parent's weakness. For this reason, the refutation of their saying ﴿اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ وَلَدًا﴾ ("Allah has taken a son") [Yunus: 68] was established by affirming that He is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani), in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿قَالُوا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ وَلَدًا ۝ سُبْحَانَهُ هُوَ الْغَنِيُّ لَهُ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ ("They say: Allah has taken a son. Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth") [Yunus: 68]. Thus, after the first verse of this surah refuted the plurality of gods in their essential and independent sense, this verse refuted the plurality of gods by way of one god being begotten from another god, because the begotten is equal to that from which it was begotten.

Plurality through begetting is equal in impossibility to plurality of gods in the essential sense, because the corruption of the cosmos that follows from plurality is the same in both cases, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿لَوْ كَانَ فِيهِمَا آلِهَةٌ إِلَّا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتَا﴾ ("Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted") [al-Anbiya': 22]. This is the proof of mutual prevention (burhan al-tamana'u). Moreover, if another existent were begotten from Allah, it would necessarily follow that a part would be separated from Allah, exalted is He, and that contradicts oneness (al-ahadiyya), as you have just known. The belief of the idolaters among the Arabs that the angels are daughters of Allah, exalted is He, was also refuted, and so they worshipped the angels on that basis, because prophethood for a god necessitates divinity for the son. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿وَقَالُوا اتَّخَذَ الرَّحْمَٰنُ وَلَدًا سُبْحَانَهُ بَلْ عِبَادٌ مُكْرَمُونَ﴾ ("They say: The Most Merciful has taken a son. Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants") [al-Anbiya': 26].

The clause ﴿وَلَمْ يُولَدْ﴾ ("nor was He begotten") is coordinated (ataf) with the clause ﴿لَمْ يَلِدْ﴾, meaning: nor was He begotten by another. It serves as a precautionary qualification (ihtiras), blocking the possibility that He might have a parent. So the negation of having a child is followed by the negation of having a parent. The negation of having a child was given priority because it is more important, since the people of error attributed a child to Allah, exalted is He, but did not attribute a parent to Allah. In this is an allusion that whoever is begotten, like Jesus, cannot be a god, for if the god were begotten, his existence would necessarily be preceded by non-existence, and that is impossible, because if he were preceded by non-existence, he would need someone to specify his existence after non-existence. Thus, from the totality of the clause ﴿لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ﴾ results the refutation that Allah be a parent of a begotten being, or be begotten of a parent, explicitly. The divinity of every begotten being was also refuted by way of implication (kinaya), so the doctrines built on the begetting of a god were refuted, such as the secondary doctrine of (Zoroaster) (Zarathustra), which holds that there are two gods: the god of good, who is the origin, and the god of evil, who is begotten from the god of good. This is because the god of good, who is called among them (Yazdan), conceived an evil thought, and from it was begotten the god of evil, who is called among them (Ahriman). Abu al-'Ala' alluded to their doctrine with his saying:

Some people said: their claim is false, so be mindful of Allah and do not assert it.
(Yazdan) thought in heedlessness, so (Ahriman) was fashioned from his thought.

The Christian doctrine of the divinity of Jesus, peace be upon him, was also refuted, since they claimed that he is the son of Allah, and that the son of Allah can only be a god. It is refuted by the fact that a god cannot have a son, so Jesus is not the son of Allah, and by the fact that a god cannot be begotten after non-existence, so what is agreed to be begotten cannot be a god, and therefore Jesus cannot be a god.

Since the first nominal clause refuted the divinity of any god other than Allah in the essential sense, and the second clause refuted the divinity of any other than Allah by right, this clause refuted the divinity of any other than Allah by derivation and begetting, by way of implication.

The negation that Allah be a parent, and that He be begotten, is in the past tense, because the doctrine of begetting claimed that this occurred in a past time, and no one claimed that Allah would take a son in the future.

[صفحة ٦١٩]

[Page 620]

In the sense of a concluding clause (tadhyil) that follows the preceding sentences, because it is more general than their content. Those preceding attributes, whether explicit, implicit or allusive, are such that no other being resembles Him in them, and this clause also conveys the negation of any likeness to Him in what lies beyond them, such as the attributes of action, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it﴾ [al-Hajj: 73].

The waw in His saying ﴿and there is none comparable to Him﴾ is parenthetical (i'tiradiyya). It is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), like the waw in Allah the Exalted's saying ﴿And do We punish any but the ungrateful?﴾ [Saba': 17], which serves as a concluding clause for ﴿That is how We recompensed them for their disbelief﴾ [Saba': 17]. It is also permissible for the waw to be conjunctive (atifa), if the first waw is taken as conjunctive. In that case the purpose of the sentence is to affirm the attribute of His being unlike created things, and the meaning of the concluding clause follows as a secondary implication, together with the subtle points, without conflict.

Kufu' (comparable, equal): it is read with a ḍamma on the kaf, a ḍamma on the fa', and a hamza at the end. This is the reading of Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far, except that the first three made the hamza clear while Abu Ja'far softened it. It is also said kuf' with a ḍamma on the kaf, a sukun on the fa', and the hamza; this is the reading of Hamza and Ya'qub. It is also said kufuwan with a waw in place of the hamza; this is the reading of Hafs from 'Asim. These are three eloquent dialectal forms.

Its meaning: the equal and the like in attributes.

Ahad (anyone) here means a human being or an existent. It is one of the indefinite nouns that are obligatorily used in the scope of negation.

Through this there arises a perfect paronomasia (jinas tamm) with His saying: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1].

The predicate of kana is placed before its subject for the sake of the rhyme-ending (fasila), and to give attention to mentioning the comparable immediately after the negated verb, so that it reaches the hearing first.

The prepositional phrase "lahu" (for Him) is placed before what it governs, which is "kufuan," to give attention to the fact that Allah deserves the negation of anyone's equality to Him. This emphasis justifies placing the prepositional phrase before its complement, even though the original order is to postpone the complement when it is an adverbial phrase of place or time. Postponing it, according to Sibawayh, is best unless something requires its advancement, as he indicated in al-Kashshaf.

Authentic and fair reports have been transmitted concerning the virtue of this surah, which the exegetes have fully collected. The sound hadith in the Muwatta' and the two Sahihs, through several chains, is established that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Say: He is Allah, the One, is equal to a third of the Qur'an."

[Page 621]

The interpretations that the scholars of the meanings of the narrations (ashab ma'ani al-athar) gave to this hadith differ, and they may be gathered into four interpretations.

The first: it is equal to a third of the Qur'an in the reward of recitation. That is, it is equal to a third of the Qur'an when the Qur'an is recited without it. So even if the reciter repeats it three times, he receives the reward of one who has recited the entire Qur'an.

The second: it is equal to a third of the Qur'an when it is recited by one who cannot recite any other surah of the Qur'an.

The third: it is equal to a third of the Qur'an with regard to the categories of meanings, since the meanings of the Qur'an are rulings, reports and tawhid. This surah is distinguished by gathering the foundations of the Islamic creed in a way no other surah gathers them.

I say: this was before the revelation of verses similar to it, such as the Verse of the Throne (ayat al-kursi), or because no single surah exists that comprises what is in Surat al-Ikhlas.

The fourth interpretation: it is equal to a third of the Qur'an in reward, as in the first interpretation, but its being recited three times is not equivalent to reciting a complete khatma (full recitation of the Qur'an).

Ibn Rushd said in al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil: The scholars have agreed that whoever recites "Say: He is Allah, the One" three times is not equal in reward to one who has revived the whole Qur'an with recitation. End. Thus this interpretation is a restriction of the first interpretation. However, his reporting of a consensus that this is what is meant is open to question, for some hadiths explicitly state that repeating it three times equals the recitation of a complete khatma.

Ibn Rushd said: Their disagreement over the interpretation of the hadith is not resolved by any of them from the problem of the hadith, nor does it escape the objection that remains in it.

Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Silence on this question is better than speaking about it.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Falaq

The Prophet (ﷺ) named this surah "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak." Al-Nasa'i related from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, who said: "I followed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was riding, and I placed my hand on his foot and said: 'Teach me, O Messenger of Allah, Surat Hud and Surat Yusuf.' He said: 'You will not recite anything more effective with Allah than "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak" and "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind."'"

This is clear that he meant the surah "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak," because it was an answer to 'Uqba's words "Teach me Surat Hud," and because he joined to "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak" the words "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind," and did not complete the surah "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak."

Al-Bukhari titled it in his Sahih "Surat Qul a'udhu bi-rabbi al-falaq," by annexing the word "surah" to the first clause of it.

Some of the Companions' speech includes naming it together with Surat al-Nas as al-Mu'awwidhatayn (the two seeking-refuge surahs). Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ahmad related from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded me to recite the mu'awwidhat," (with a shadda on the waw of the feminine form, in the plural, taking the verses as al-mu'awwidhat, that is, the verses of the two surahs). In another narration: "with the two mu'awwidhatayn after every prayer." None of the exegetes mentioned that either of them is called al-mu'awwidha in the singular. Ibn 'Atiyya called it "the first mu'awwidha surah," so the annexation of "surah" to "mu'awwidha" is an annexation of the named to the name, and describing the surah by this is metaphorical, as if it guides the fearful to the place that protects him from what frightens him, or as if it admits him into a place of refuge.

It is named in most mushafs and the majority of exegetical books "Surat al-Falaq."

In al-Itqan it is stated that it and Surat al-Nas are called al-mushaqshiqatayn (with the two shins placed before the two qafs), from the phrase "a khatib mushaqshiq" (an eloquent speaker whose words flow), comparing him to a noble male camel that roars with a shaqshaqa, which is like flesh that protrudes from its mouth when it is angry. End. I have not verified the reason for describing the two mu'awwidhatayn by this.

In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi and in al-Kashshaf, it is said that it and Surat al-Nas are called al-muqashqishatayn (with the qaf placed before the two shins). Al-Qurtubi added: that is, they absolve one of hypocrisy. Al-Tibi said likewise. Thus the name al-muqashqisha is shared among four surahs: this one, Surat al-Nas, Surat Bara'a (al-Tawbah), and Surat al-Kafirun.

Scholars disputed whether it is Meccan or Medinan. Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, 'Ata' and 'Ikrima said it is Meccan, and Kurayb related it from Ibn 'Abbas. Qatada said it is Medinan, and Abu Salih related it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The more correct view is that it is Meccan, because Kurayb's report from Ibn 'Abbas is accepted, unlike Abu Salih's report from Ibn 'Abbas, which is subject to criticism.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said it was revealed because Labid ibn al-A'sam had bewitched the Prophet (ﷺ). The Sahih collections do not state that it was revealed for this reason. The author of al-Itqan based on this his preference that the surah is Medinan. We will discuss the story of Labid ibn al-A'sam when we reach the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾ [al-Falaq: 4].

It has also been said that the reason for its revelation, and that of the surah after it, is that the Quraysh incited (nadabu), that is, they incited those known among them to strike the Prophet (ﷺ) with the evil eye. So Allah revealed the two mu'awwidhatayn so that he might seek refuge from them through them. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) reported this from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, but did not give its chain.

It is counted among the twentieth surahs in order of revelation: it was revealed after Surat al-Fil and before Surat al-Nas.

The number of its verses is five by agreement.

It is well known from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud in the Sahih that he used to deny that the two mu'awwidhatayn are part of the Qur'an, and he would say: "The Messenger of Allah was only commanded to seek refuge with them," that is, he was not commanded to regard them as part of the Qur'an. However, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed on reciting them in prayer, and they were written in their mushafs, and it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited them in his prayer.

* * *

The purpose of this surah is to teach the Prophet (ﷺ) words for seeking refuge in Allah from the evil of harmful created beings whose evil is to be feared, from times in which evil frequently occurs, and from situations in which the nature of evil is concealed behind them, so that their perpetrators are not blamed for its consequences. Allah taught His Prophet this refuge-seeking surah so that he might seek refuge with it. It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to seek refuge with this surah and its companion, and he commanded his Companions to seek refuge with the two of them. Thus seeking refuge with them became part of the Sunnah of the Muslims.
